declared.title: Subjective Well-Being and Income: Is There Any Evidence of Satiation?
declared.foundIn: OpenAlex search « subjective well-being and income is there any evidence of satiation » (2026-11-22)

population: people and countries in several surveys: Gallup World Poll 2008-2012 (155 countries, Egypt among them), World Values Survey, Pew, ISSP, US Gallup

findings.text: Testing the claim that income stops mattering once basic needs are met, across rich and poor countries and people, finds no support for it

support.sentence: Analyzing multiple datasets, multiple definitions of "basic needs" and multiple questions about well-being, we find no support for this claim.

findings.text: Well-being rises by the same step for each doubling of income, and that step does not shrink among the rich

support.sentence: The relationship between well-being and income is roughly log-linear and does not diminish as incomes rise.

limits: cross-sectional: an association, not an effect of money
Egypt (NBER w18992): a national mean (fig. 1), then life evaluation vs household income inside Egypt, 10th-90th income percentiles (fig. 2)
Egypt again in fig. 3: the slope above vs below $15,000 of household income, one of 98 countries; MENA neighbours there too
the thresholds tested between and within countries are basic-needs levels ($8,000 to $25,000); only a US poll (incomes up to $500,000) tests high incomes
evaluative measures only (ladder, satisfaction): says nothing about day-to-day emotions
« log-linear » means each extra dollar still adds less: it contradicts a plateau, not diminishing returns
